sections.title: Challenges Faced by People Living in Forests
Government Efforts to Support Forest Dwellers

slides.title: Forests Feed Livelihoods
slides.kicker: Jungle sirf ped nahi, roti bhi hai!
bullets: People, particularly rural and tribal communities, rely heavily on forests for their livelihoods.
Forests provide essential resources such as food, fuel, fodder, medicine, shelter, timber, bamboo, and firewood.
Forests also support livestock grazing, small forest-based industries, ecotourism, and employment.
slides.note: Jungle hi dukaan, dawa khana aur ghar hai!

slides.title: Non-Timber Forest Products
slides.kicker: Shahad aur mahua bhi kamai hai!
bullets: Non-timber forest products include honey, fruits, nuts, resins, and medicinal plants.
These products help forest families meet daily needs and earn income.
Jharkhand and Odisha are known for wild fruits, honey, mushrooms, and roots.
Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh supply tendu leaves, mahua flowers, sal seeds, and gums.
slides.note: Gathering bhi ek professional skill hai!

slides.title: Sacred Groves of India
bullets: Sacred groves are small forest patches protected by local communities for religious and cultural purposes.
Across India there are over 1,00,000 sacred groves, though many are not officially recorded.
They are known by different names such as Devrai, Devarakadu, Kavu, and Sarna.
Despite being small, they preserve rare plants, medicinal species, and wildlife, and some maintain streams and groundwater.
slides.note: Kitne groves tumne ab tak dekhe?

slides.title: Faith Meets Sustainability
bullets: Communities including the Gonds and Bhils perform rituals to honour forest deities before collecting resources.
Such rituals reflect sustainable cultural practices and a deep respect for nature.
Forest dwellers rely on forests for household needs, cultural practices, and livelihood activities.
Women play a vital role in collecting and managing forest resources, sustaining traditional knowledge and practices.

slides.title: What is a GI Tag
bullets: A Geographical Indication (GI) tag is an intellectual property right that identifies a product as originating from a specific place.
A given quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the product is essentially linked to its geographic origin.
In simple terms, it is a label showing that a product comes from a particular region and gets its uniqueness from that place.
slides.note: GI matlab product ka address proof!

slides.title: Why GI Tagging Matters
slides.kicker: Gaon ka naam, duniya tak pehchaan!
bullets: GI tagging helps protect region-specific products from losing their identity.
It promotes the cultural heritage tied to a place and its traditions.
It generates economic benefits for local communities through exclusive market recognition.

slides.title: GI Honey, Litchi, Toys
slides.kicker: Shahad se khilone tak, sab GI!
bullets: Ramban Sulai Honey of Jammu and Kashmir has strong antioxidant and immuno-modulatory potential and a distinct flavour, aroma, and taste.
Tezpur Litchi of Assam grows in forest-influenced soil and climate, with a distinctive bright colour and high pulp content.
Channapatna Toys of Karnataka are made from Wrightia tinctoria, a forest tree locally known as Aale mara.

items: Ramban Sulai Honey: nutrition and antioxidants

slides.title: Turmeric, Tea, Fruits
slides.kicker: Haldi se chai tak, sab apne!
bullets: Kandhamal Haldi of Odisha is grown by tribal communities in forest regions and is known for high curcumin content and medicinal value.
Erode Turmeric of Tamil Nadu is cultivated in forest-influenced soils and is used for cooking and ayurvedic medicine.
Nilgiri Tea is plantation-based, yet its quality depends on the forest ecosystem conditions of the Western Ghats.
Tripura Queen Pineapple is famous for sweetness and aroma, while Khasi Mandarin is a citrus fruit from the forest-rich hills of Meghalaya.
slides.note: Mitti bhi jungle se, swad bhi!

slides.title: Daily Struggles in Forests
bullets: People living in forests often struggle to access essential facilities such as healthcare, education, and clean water.
Women are exposed to fuelwood fumes and face many health issues, making their daily lives difficult.
Forest dwellers depend heavily on forest produce such as firewood, honey, bamboo, and medicinal plants for their livelihood.
slides.note: PMUY kaise badlega yeh soorat? Socho!

slides.title: Blocked Access, Lost Income
bullets: Restrictions on forest use, deforestation, and commercial exploitation often limit forest dwellers' access to resources.
This creates a conflict between conservation laws and their survival needs, leading to economic insecurity.
Many forest dwellers face discrimination and neglect, and often sell forest products at relatively low prices.
Processing and marketing opportunities, help with government schemes, and awareness of legal rights are essential to raise incomes.

slides.title: Disasters and Forest Fires
bullets: Floods in forested hilly regions wash away homes, crops, and roads, while landslides can bury villages and cut off essential services.
Forest fires spread quickly through dense vegetation, destroying homes and resources; human care and preventive measures can prevent many.
As per the Forest Survey of India, about 36 per cent of the country's forest cover is prone to fires, nearly 4 per cent extremely prone.
Climate change as well as human-induced factors are the main reasons for such occurrences.
slides.note: 4 per cent bahut bada number hai!

slides.title: Wildlife Conflict and Fairness
slides.kicker: Haathi bhi, kisan bhi, dono yaad rakhna!
bullets: Crops are often damaged by elephants, monkeys, or wild boars, and sometimes people face direct attacks.
Such conflicts cause economic losses and create fear and insecurity among forest communities.
Forest dwellers often sell their products at low prices, so opportunities for processing and marketing are essential to enhance income.
Communities also require assistance in accessing government schemes and greater awareness of their legal rights.

left.title: Human-wildlife conflict
items: Crops damaged by elephants, monkeys, and wild boars

slides.title: The Forest Rights Act 2006
bullets: The Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, is the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act.
It recognises the rights of eligible communities over the forest land and resources they have traditionally depended upon.
It allows them to collect minor forest produce such as bamboo, honey, and medicinal plants.
It also grants ownership of small patches of land cultivated by them.

slides.title: Schemes and Programmes
bullets: The Government runs tribal welfare schemes including education scholarships, healthcare programmes, and skill development initiatives.
The Joint Forest Management (JFM) programme encourages local communities to protect forests while benefiting from forest produce.
PESA, the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DAJGUA) are other initiatives.
PM JANMAN, the Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan, also aims to promote the welfare of such communities.

slides.title: Mendha Lekha: First FRA Village
slides.kicker: Mawa Nate Mawa Raj, gaon ka raj!
bullets: Mendha Lekha is a small tribal village in the Gadchiroli district of Maharashtra, inhabited mainly by the Gond tribe.
It became the first village in India to gain rights over its forest resources under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
The village follows the principle of Mawa Nate Mawa Raj, meaning our village, our rule.
All decisions are made collectively through the Gram Sabha.

slides.title: 1,800 Hectares, One Community
bullets: The people of Mendha Lekha protect and sustainably utilise 1,800 hectares of forest.
They regulate tree cutting, prevent forest fires, and promote bamboo harvesting as a renewable resource.
Revenue from forest produce funds community welfare activities such as education and infrastructure.
Villagers uphold their right to join governance and their duty of protecting biodiversity and preventing illegal exploitation.

slides.title: Think Like a Geographer
bullets: The chapter asks why India has diverse biomes and how local geography connects to this diversity.
Factors like temperature, precipitation patterns, and dominant plant species decide which biome develops in a region.
It also asks why forests are called the lungs of the Earth; forests maintain oxygen levels and balance the Earth's climate.
slides.note: Geography se hi jawab milta hai!

slides.title: Your Field Projects
slides.kicker: Apne ilaqe ka survey khud karo!
bullets: List economically valuable native plants in your region and comment on their abundance.
Prepare a map of your state or Union Territory showing national parks and sanctuaries.
Discuss traditional forest conservation methods with your grandparents or an elderly person.

slides.title: Fire, Climate, Community Guardians
bullets: Study the impact of forest fires on people dependent on forests: their causes, losses, and preventive measures.
The chapter asks what long-term effect the destruction of large forest areas would have on the global climate.
Forest dwellers help protect forests through sacred groves, community rules in Mendha Lekha, and Joint Forest Management.

examples.title: From Forest to Family Income
examples.problem: Rani's family lives near a forest in Chhattisgarh. Using the chapter, describe how forests support their household: name at least three resources, two non-timber forest products they could gather, and one cultural practice that keeps this use sustainable.
steps: Identify household resources: forests provide food, fuel, fodder, medicine, shelter, timber, bamboo, and firewood.
Pick the non-timber products: honey, fruits, nuts, resins, and medicinal plants help families meet daily needs and earn income.
Match the state map: Chhattisgarh is listed for tendu leaves, mahua flowers, sal seeds, and gums.
Add the sustainability layer: like the Gonds and Bhils, the family performs rituals to honour forest deities before collecting resources.
examples.answer: Forests meet Rani's family's needs through resources like fuel and fodder and products like tendu leaves and mahua flowers, while rituals before collection keep the use sustainable.

examples.title: Be a GI Detective
examples.problem: A product is grown by tribal communities in the forest regions of Kandhamal, has high curcumin content, and is valued for medicinal use. Identify the GI-tagged product and its state, and state what its GI tag achieves.
steps: Clue one: grown by tribal communities in forest regions points to a forest-based product.
Clue two: high curcumin content and medicinal value point to a turmeric variety.
Match with the GI list in the book: Kandhamal Haldi from Odisha fits all the clues.
Recall what a GI tag does: it protects region-specific products, promotes cultural heritage, and generates economic benefits through exclusive market recognition.
examples.answer: Kandhamal Haldi from Odisha; its GI tag certifies its origin-linked quality and brings protection, recognition, and income to local communities.

examples.title: How Fire-Prone Is This Forest?
examples.problem: A district has 500 square kilometres of forest cover. As a model calculation using the Forest Survey of India estimates given in the book, find how much of this area is prone to forest fires and how much is extremely prone.
steps: The book states that about 36 per cent of the country's forest cover is prone to forest fires.
Prone area: 36 per cent of 500 = 0.36 x 500 = 180 square kilometres.
The book adds that nearly 4 per cent of this fire-prone cover is extremely prone: 4 per cent of 180 = 7.2 square kilometres.
Check the remainder: 500 - 180 = 320 square kilometres is relatively less prone.
examples.answer: About 180 square kilometres is prone to forest fires, of which nearly 7.2 square kilometres is extremely prone.

examples.title: Plan Like Mendha Lekha
examples.problem: Your village Gram Sabha wants to manage its community forest the way Mendha Lekha does. Draft the main steps of the plan using the case study from the chapter.
steps: Adopt the principle of Mawa Nate Mawa Raj: take every decision collectively through the Gram Sabha.
Protect the forest by regulating tree cutting and preventing forest fires.
Promote bamboo harvesting as a renewable resource so the forest keeps regenerating.
Use the revenue from forest produce for community welfare activities such as education and infrastructure.
examples.answer: A Gram Sabha-led plan that protects the forest, harvests bamboo sustainably, and reinvests revenue in education and infrastructure, balancing rights with duties.
